beliefs.practice: Never commit the cluster connection string or credentials to source control; read the DocumentDB connection URI and credentials from environment variables (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime and optionally store secrets in Azure Key Vault. Do not log the raw connection string.

Use a dedicated database and well‑named collections for the app (e.g., use database sample_healthcare_11 and create separate collections for patients and visits) rather than writing into shared or admin databases.

Choose an appropriate partition key with high cardinality (e.g., patient_id for visits) so related documents are co‑located and to avoid hot partitions; design collections so typical aggregations and lookups operate efficiently within partitions when possible.

For seeding large datasets, use bulk writes (bulk_write / insert_many with ordered=False) and tune batch sizes to avoid large single‑document/large‑transaction overhead; monitor RU consumption while seeding.

Create indexes that support the aggregation pipeline: ensure fields used in $match and $sort (age/dob, diagnosis codes, last_visit_date, patient_id) are indexed with appropriate single or compound indexes (e.g., {patient_id:1, last_visit_date:-1}).
Project only required fields in queries and aggregation ($project early) to reduce network and memory usage, and push $match as early as possible in pipelines so indexes can be used.

When performing heavy aggregations, use explain() and the MCP server tools to inspect the aggregation plan and confirm index usage; if an aggregation will produce large intermediate data, use allowDiskUse or write intermediate results to a collection ($out/$merge).

Implement retries with exponential backoff for transient errors (network timeouts, 429 / rate limit responses). Make writes idempotent when retries are used (e.g., upsert with a deterministic _id or idempotency key).

Configure the MongoDB driver connection pool (maxPoolSize, minPoolSize) and timeouts (connectTimeoutMS, socketTimeoutMS) appropriate for your concurrency; reuse a global client instance rather than creating a new client per request.

Use TLS/SSL for all connections to the cluster (enable ssl=true/ tls=true in connection string) and verify server certificates; prefer private endpoints or VNet integration to avoid exposing the cluster to public internet.

Apply the principle of least privilege: create a database user with only the required roles (e.g., readWrite on sample_healthcare_11) for the app and avoid using the cluster admin key for regular application operations.

For PHI and healthcare data, do not send identifiable patient data to third‑party LLMs unless you have a HIPAA‑compliant contract and proper de‑identification; prefer on‑prem or private LLMs or redact sensitive fields before calling external APIs.

Monitor RU consumption, latency, index usage and throughput with Azure Monitor and set autoscale or adequate provisioned throughput to avoid 429s during batch loads or heavy aggregations; test expected workloads against the cluster size (M30) before production use.

For vector search, store embeddings as dense float arrays in a dedicated field and create the appropriate vector index (choose index type matching workload: HNSW for high‑recall, IVF/DiskANN for large scale); normalize vectors if using cosine similarity.

When combining patient and visit data, prefer an approach that supports your query patterns: embed recent visits into patient documents for fast reads of the latest visit; use a separate visits collection if visits grow unbounded and require their own indexes/partitions.

Avoid operations that return extremely large documents or unbounded result sets; always use pagination (limit/skip or better yet range queries with a sort key) and set reasonable batchSize on cursors to control memory and RU usage.

Use server‑side aggregation ($group/$lookup/$facet) to reduce clientside joins when possible, but ensure supporting indexes exist for the $lookup local/foreign fields; prefer pipeline optimizations (pre-filtering) to reduce data shuffled in joins.
Audit and enable diagnostics/logging: capture slow query logs, Azure diagnostic settings, index usage and failed requests to inform index tuning and cost control.

Use explain() and indexStats to validate that compound indexes are being used by the aggregation and query shapes you deploy; favor compound indexes that support both the $match and subsequent $sort to avoid in‑memory sorts.
Protect backups and enable customer‑managed keys (CMK) for encryption at rest when handling regulated healthcare data; verify restore/test procedures and retention policies.

Tune indexes for cardinality: avoid indexing low‑cardinality boolean flags unless used heavily in selective queries; consider partial or sparse indexes if supported to reduce index size for fields like diagnosis codes where only a subset of docs have values.

When seeding or running schema‑changing operations, run them first against a staging/test database on the same cluster size (same M30 tier) to observe RU, index build time and query plans before applying to production data.

If the app issues long aggregations or analytic workloads, consider precomputing care‑gap flags as materialized results (periodic batch jobs writing to a prioritized outreach collection) rather than computing ad‑hoc for every user request.

Use driver‑level options for retryable reads/writes where supported (retryReads/retryWrites) and be aware of differences in retry semantics between MongoDB drivers and Azure's MongoDB API; test retry behavior for your driver version.
